title: Learned Optimism
note: DB Turkish title 'İyimserlik Öğrenmek'. Original English title Learned Optimism (Knopf, 1990). Full text was not accessible; facts rest on Seligman's own papers (1967 triadic design via Maier & Seligman 2016 review; Seligman & Schulman 1986 Met Life paper), his interviews, and multiple book summaries/reader highlights. Exact book wording is not quoted.

facts.claim: In the mid-1960s at the University of Pennsylvania, dogs given tone-paired shocks in a hammock were later put in a shuttlebox where escape needed only a jump over a low barrier; many did not escape and passively waited the shock out.

Seligman and Steven Maier's triadic design (published 1967): one group could end the shock by pressing a panel with the nose; a yoked group received exactly the same shocks but nothing it did had any effect; a third group received no shock.
In the shuttlebox, about two-thirds of the yoked (inescapable) animals failed to learn to escape, while about 90% of the escapable and no-shock animals learned it easily.

Donald Hiroto ran a human version: loud noise that could be stopped by pressing buttons, the same noise with no control, or no noise; afterwards in a new task where moving a hand turned the noise off, most of the no-control group did not try; some said nothing had worked, so why try.

About one in three people could not be made helpless in the lab; Seligman says this made him ask what made them resilient, which led to explanatory style. About one in ten seemed helpless from the start.
facts.source: NPR 2020 interview (one-third, Seligman's own words); one-in-ten via secondary column

facts.claim: Seligman named the phenomenon learned helplessness and linked it to depression.

Caveat: in 2016 Maier and Seligman wrote that 'the original theory got it backwards': passivity under prolonged shock is the default, unlearned response; what is learned is control, detected by the medial prefrontal cortex.

Explanatory style has three dimensions: permanence (always vs. this time), pervasiveness (everything vs. this area), personalization (me vs. circumstances). Pessimists explain bad events as permanent, pervasive and their own fault; optimists as temporary, specific and not wholly their fault. For good events the pattern reverses: optimists see successes as permanent, pervasive and their own doing.
facts.source: book summaries; Goodreads highlights of Learned Optimism

facts.claim: Met Life: agents scoring in the top half on Seligman's Attributional Style Questionnaire sold 37% more insurance in their first two years than those in the bottom half; in a second study, top-half scorers stayed in the job at twice the rate of bottom-half scorers.
Met Life president John Creedon turned to Seligman because the company lost many new agents to quitting; selling insurance involves repeated rejection.

A 'special force' of 129 applicants who failed the industry career-profile test but scored as strong optimists was hired; they outsold the pessimists in the regular force by 21% in the first year and 57% in the second.
facts.source: Fortune excerpt quoted by waldentesting; ThinkAdvisor

facts.claim: The ABC model comes from Albert Ellis: Adversity, Belief, Consequence. Seligman adds D (Disputation) and E (Energization). Feelings and actions (C) follow from the belief (B) about the adversity, not from the adversity alone.
The reader is asked to record ABC episodes from daily life over a few days to see the belief between event and reaction.

Disputation has four tacks: Evidence, Alternatives, Implications (even if true, is it a catastrophe?), Usefulness. Where disputing is not possible in the moment, distraction or scheduling a later time to think it over.
Seligman suggests disputing your own pessimistic thought as if a third person whose job is to make your life miserable, or a rival for your job, had said it.

rejected.claim: Depression is usually not a chemical problem but learned helplessness.
rejected.reason: Overstated; not a supported claim attributable to the book in this form.
